Merely to read about the splendours enjoyed by the dead was marvellous.

Next his interest passed to embroideries and those tapestries which served in place of frescoes in the cold chambers of northern Europe. While pursuing this study—and he possessed a remarkable gift for surrendering himself entirely, for the moment, to any subject he undertook—he felt almost sorrowful at the thought of the destruction time inflicted upon lovely and extraordinary things. He, at least, had eluded it. Summer succeeded summer; again and again the yellow jonquils flowered and withered; nights of terror repeated their shameful tale; yet he remained the same. No winter injured his face or dimmed its blossom-like freshness. How otherwise it was with material possessions! Where had they gone? What had become of the immense crocus-hued robe upon which gods battled giants, embroidered by brown maidens to delight Athena? Where was Nero's enormous velarium over the Roman Colosseum, that gigantic purple sail displaying the star-filled heavens and Apollo in a chariot pulled by white horses with gilded reins? He yearned to behold the strange table-napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, showing every delicacy and dish a banquet could require; King Chilperic's burial cloth, adorned with three hundred bees of gold; the fantastic garments which had provoked the Bishop of Pontus, covered in “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters”—everything, indeed, that an artist might imitate from nature. He wished to see the coat once worn by Charles of Orleans, its sleeves embroidered with the lines of a song beginning “Madame, je suis tout joyeux,” the accompanying music traced in golden thread, each note—square in that age—fashioned from four pearls. He read about the chamber prepared for Queen Joan of Burgundy in the palace at Rheims, decorated with thirteen hundred and twenty-one embroidered parrots bearing the king's arms and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies whose wings similarly bore the queen's arms, all executed in gold. Catherine de Medicis commissioned a mourning-bed of black velvet scattered with suns and crescents. Damask curtains showed leafy wreaths and garlands against a ground of silver and gold, their borders fringed with pearl embroidery. The bed stood in a room hung with repeated rows of the queen's emblems, cut in black velvet and applied to silver cloth. In the apartment of Louis XIV stood caryatides fifteen feet tall, embroidered in gold.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, Somersetshire, read only one book for pleasure: the Baronetage, the record of baronets and their families. It occupied him when he was idle and comforted him when he was troubled. Reading about the few surviving families whose titles were among the oldest filled him with admiration and respect. Any unpleasant feelings caused by family affairs turned to pity and contempt as he looked through the almost endless titles created in the previous century. If no other page helped, he could always read his own history with unfailing interest. His favorite book naturally opened at this entry:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park in Gloucestershire, on July 15, 1784. Their children were Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a stillborn son, November 5, 1789; and Mary, born November 20, 1791. His wife died in 1800.”

That was the information originally printed. Sir Walter had improved it for his own and his family's benefit by adding after Mary's birth date: “Married on December 16, 1810, to Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross, Somersetshire.” He had also carefully inserted the exact day of the month on which his wife died.

Next came the history and rise of this old, respectable family, described in the usual terms. It told how they first settled in Cheshire and were mentioned in Dugdale; how family members served as high sheriff, represented a borough in three successive parliaments, displayed loyalty, and received a baronetcy in the first year of Charles II. It included all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. Altogether, it filled two handsome pages of the small volume and ended with the family arms and motto, followed by “Principal residence: Kellynch Hall, Somersetshire.” Sir Walter's handwriting supplied one last addition:

“Expected heir: William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity defined Sir Walter Elliot completely: pride in both his appearance and his rank. He had been exceptionally handsome when young and remained a very fine-looking man at fifty-four. Few women cared more about their looks, and no newly created lord's valet could have taken more pleasure in his social position. Sir Walter considered beauty a blessing second only to a baronetcy. Possessing both, he constantly gave himself his warmest respect and devotion.

His good looks and rank did deserve his gratitude in one respect. They must have won him a wife whose character was far better than his own deserved.

We shared our love for Adrian, although she, still scarcely beyond childhood, could not appreciate the full range of his qualities as I did, or feel the same sympathy with his interests and beliefs. I was constantly in his company. His sensitivity and sweetness gave our conversations a tender, almost unearthly quality. He could be as joyful as a lark singing high in the sky, as soaring in thought as an eagle, and as innocent as a gentle-eyed dove. He could lighten Perdita's seriousness and ease the painful restlessness of my nature. I looked back on my unsettled desires and bitter struggles with other people as though remembering a troubled dream. I felt so transformed that I might have entered another body, whose fresh senses and nerves changed the image of the visible universe reflected in my mind. Yet that was not what had happened. My strength remained, as did my deep need for sympathy and my longing for active effort. My manly virtues had not abandoned me: the enchantress Urania had spared Samson's hair as he rested at her feet. But everything was gentler and more humane. Nor did Adrian teach me only the detached truths of history and philosophy. While using them to help me restrain my reckless, untrained spirit, he also opened the living pages of his own heart, allowing me to feel and understand its extraordinary nature.

Even when her son was an infant, the former queen of England had tried to plant bold, ambitious plans in his mind. Recognizing his genius and exceptional talents, she cultivated them so that she could later use them to advance her own aims. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his impulsive courage. She even tolerated his ungovernable love of freedom, hoping that, as happens all too often, it would develop into a desire to rule. She tried to raise him to resent those who had helped bring about his father's abdication and to want revenge on them. In this she failed. However distorted the accounts he received, the story of a great and wise nation asserting its right to govern itself awakened his admiration. From an early age, he became a republican by conviction. Still, his mother refused to despair. Along with her love of power and arrogant pride in her birth, she possessed determined ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying her son's character. Through praise, criticism, and persuasion, she tried to find and strike the right chords. Although the music produced by her touch sounded discordant to her, she rested her hopes on his talents and remained certain that she would eventually win him over.
